summary: Describes a language tag for indicating the language used in an information object. It is on the standards track. It has been replaced by RFC 3066 and RFC 3282.

eli5.summary: A short label, like en or fr, that says what language some text is in.

questions: how to identify language of content
subtitle: The original scheme for labelling content with a language, such as en or en-US, plus the Content-Language header.

tldr.problem: People prefer information in a language they understand, but there was no standard way to label content with the language it is written in.
tldr.mechanism: A language tag is a primary tag plus optional subtags, each of 1 to 8 letters, joined by hyphens. Two-letter primary tags follow ISO 639, and the RFC adds a Content-Language header and a differences parameter for multipart/alternative.
tldr.outcome: The RFC was replaced by RFC 3066 and RFC 3282.

today: RFC 1766 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 3066 and RFC 3282, so those are the documents to follow instead.

sections.title: The Language Tag
sections.content:
A language tag has one or more parts: a primary tag and a possibly empty series of subtags. In the RFC's EBNF: Language-Tag = Primary-tag *( "-" Subtag ), with both the primary tag and each subtag being 1 to 8 letters. Whitespace is not allowed in a tag, and tags are case insensitive. The convention of lowercase language and uppercase country (for example en-US) is recommended but carries no meaning.

The primary tag has fixed meanings: any two-letter tag is interpreted under ISO 639, the value i is reserved for IANA-defined registrations, and x is reserved for private use. No other values can be assigned without updating the standard.

In the first subtag, two-letter codes are ISO 3166 country codes, and codes of 3 to 8 letters can be registered with IANA by anyone. Later subtags can be any registered value. Examples given are a country (en-US), a dialect or variant (no-nynorsk, en-cockney), a language missing from ISO 639 (i-cherokee) and a script (az-arabic, az-cyrillic). The RFC says none of its example subtags have actually been assigned.
sections.eli5: A tag is like a short label: a main word for the language, then optional extra bits for the country or special version, joined with dashes. Capital letters do not matter.

sections.title: What a Tag Means
sections.content:
A tag always names a language spoken or written by people to communicate with other people. Computer languages are explicitly excluded.

Tags that begin with the same subtags are not guaranteed to be mutually comprehensible, so applications should treat a tag as a single token. Splitting it into main tag and subtags is an administrative mechanism, not a navigation aid.

How a tag relates to content depends on the context. For one object it means the set of languages needed to understand it fully. For a collection such as a library, it means the languages used inside the parts. For a set of alternatives, it is a hint that the material is offered in several languages, so a reader need not know them all.
sections.eli5: A tag says which human language something is in, not a computer language. Two tags that start the same do not always mean people can understand each other.

sections.title: The Content-Language Header
sections.content:
The Content-Language header marks the language of anything with RFC 822-style headers, such as MIME body parts or Web documents. Its grammar is Language-Header = "Content-Language" ":" 1#Language-tag, so it may list several tags separated by commas. Whitespace and parenthesized comments are allowed.

Examples from the RFC include Content-Language: en-cockney for a recording from the London docks, Content-Language: en, fr (This is a dictionary) for an English-French dictionary, and x-klingon for a Star Trek excerpt.
sections.eli5: It is a line at the top of a message that says which language the message is in. It can list more than one language.

sections.title: Multipart/Alternative and the Differences Parameter
sections.content:
In MIME multipart/alternative, body parts can carry the same content in different languages. The RFC says to put a Content-Language header on each part and a summary header on the whole.

Since a normal reader will not choose the part by language, the RFC defines a new parameter, Differences, whose value is one or more of Content-Type and Content-Language. Further values can be registered with IANA, and if the parameter is absent, Differences=Content-Type is assumed. How the reader picks which part to show is out of scope.

When composing, non-MIME mail readers show the first body part first, so it should be the language most recipients understand.
sections.eli5: Sometimes one message carries the same text in several languages. This adds a note telling mail programs to choose by language, so you get the one you can read.

sections.title: Registration and Other Considerations
sections.content:
A new tag must start with an existing tag and extend it. A requester fills out a registration form giving name, email, the tag, the English and native names of the language, and a reference to a published description. The form goes to a mailing list for a 2-week review, then a language tag reviewer appointed by the IETF Applications Area Director either forwards it to IANA or rejects it for significant objections. Decisions can be appealed to the IESG.

Security issues are not discussed in the memo. For character sets, codes can always be written in US-ASCII letters. The RFC also notes that picking a rendering based on the tag cannot work in every case, for example mixed Japanese and Chinese text.
sections.eli5: To add a new language label, you fill in a form, people have two weeks to comment, and a reviewer then approves it or says no.

data.title: multipart/alternative by language
data.code:
Content-Type: multipart/alternative; differences=Content-Language;
          boundary="limit"
Content-Language: en, fr, de

--limit
Content-Language: fr

Le renard brun et agile saute par dessus le chien paresseux
--limit
Content-Language: de

Der schnelle braune Fuchs h=FCpft =FCber den faulen Hund
--limit
Content-Language: en

The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog
--limit--
